newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-CHAPMAN STILL LEADS ENGLISH OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-CHAPMAN STILL LEADS ENGLISH OPEN.

text.p: England's Roger Chapman, who has had six European Tour runner-up places but never a victory in 16 years, led the English Open for a second day on Thursday, boosted by a spectacular eagle
Chapman, 38, holed out with a five iron from 183 yards out at Hanbury Manor's par-four 10th on his way to a second consecutive six-under-par 66 to take a one-stroke lead on 132, 12 under par.

He denied himself a bigger lead by bogeying the last in an enigmatic round which included the eagle and eight birdies but also four dropped shots at regular intervals after also erring at the first hole.

His see-saw performance maintained his lead in the face of a big finish by Sweden's Dennis Edlund, who found his eagle at the par-five ninth, his closing hole, to climb into second place on 11-under with a 65. Chapman's young compatriot Steve Webster took up third place on 10-under after a 66.

On a day of record-breaking, American Jay Townsend fired the best of the week as the 35-year-old, who hunts bears in his spare time, clawed up to fourth place. Townsend's nine-birdie 63 bettered the record 64s set by Jose Coceres of Argentina and Northern Ireland's Darren Clarke earlier, the pair having broken the old record by two shots.

Clarke's 64 took him to a share of fifth spot on eight-under, with Coceres a further stroke back. Overnight second-placed Thomas Goegele was also seven- under. Reigning European No. 1 Colin Montgomerie of Scotland had his best round for some time, shooting a 68 to move four-under, one ahead of comeback Spaniard Jose Maria Olazabal who had to settle for 72. Defending champion Robert Allenby crashed out of the tournament, failing to make the two-under-par cut by three strokes, not helped by double-bogeying the 18th, the Australian's ninth hole, on his way to posting 72.

Leader Chapman needed the steadying influence of his caddie after he had eagled the 10th, being told to 'focus on the shot in hand and forget about the hole before' and it paid dividends as he birdied the next hole. And Chapman admits he relies on others as props.

He praised his coach for getting his swing right for the week and his new sports psychologist Chris Linstead, a British martial arts expert who also helped Europe's Ryder Cup team in 1995, for helping him to think positive, and yesterday it was also the turn of a putting 'doctor' another Briton, Dean Wingrove. "You surround yourself with positive people and you can get it right," said Chapman. "Dean gave me a putting lesson last night and it worked because I had a great putting round. Chris told me to forget my 66 of the first day and think of the present not the past, stay 100 per cent focused on the job in hand." Chapman, who once owned a failed racehorse called 'Pepper the Pin', likened his weekend task to the British horserace, the Grand National. "I'm over Beecher's Brook but now I've got Valentine's and The Chair to come," he added.ends
